questions.question: What is the difference between widening and narrowing type conversion in Java?
questions.title: Widening vs Narrowing Type Conversion in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Widening conversion** is implicit — smaller type to larger type (int → long → double). No data loss, done automatically by Java. **Narrowing conversion** is explicit — larger type to smaller type (double → int), requires a cast, and may cause data loss through truncation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's type system and automatic vs manual conversions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that narrowing truncates (doesn't round) — (int) 3.9 gives 3, not 4
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the widening order: byte → short → int → long → float → double, and explain why data loss happens in narrowing

sections.title: Widening and Narrowing Conversions
Widening vs Narrowing
sections.content:
| Aspect | Widening | Narrowing |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Small → Large | Large → Small |
| Cast required | No (automatic) | Yes (explicit) |
| Data loss | No | Possible (truncation/overflow) |
| Example | int → long | double → int |
| Runtime error | Never | No error — silent data loss |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Widening conversion goes from a smaller type to a larger one — like int to long or int to double. Java does this automatically because there's no risk of losing data; the larger type can always hold any value the smaller type had. Narrowing is the opposite — you're going from a larger type to a smaller one, so you must explicitly cast it with parentheses. The key gotcha with narrowing is truncation: if you cast 3.9 to int, you get 3, not 4 — the decimal part is just thrown away. And if the value overflows the target type, you get a wraparound which can give you a completely unexpected number.

questions.question: What is ClassCastException in Java and when does it occur?
questions.title: ClassCastException in Java — Object Type Casting
questions.direct_answer: **`ClassCastException`** is a runtime exception thrown when you try to cast an object to a type it isn't actually an instance of. Downcasting (parent reference to child type) can cause this if the actual object is not of the target type. Use `instanceof` before casting to prevent it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of object casting and runtime type safety in Java's type system
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Performing downcasts without instanceof check, or not understanding that upcasting is always safe but downcasting is not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between upcasting (always safe, implicit) and downcasting (potentially unsafe, explicit), and mention the Java 16+ pattern matching instanceof

sections.title: ClassCastException — When Casting Goes Wrong
Key Points
sections.content:
- `ClassCastException` is a **runtime** exception (not compile-time)
- Upcasting (child → parent) is always safe and automatic
- Downcasting (parent → child) requires explicit cast and can throw ClassCastException
- Always use `instanceof` before downcasting
- Java 16+ pattern matching: `if (obj instanceof Dog d)` combines check and cast
- The compiler allows the cast syntactically even if it will fail at runtime

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ClassCastException happens when you try to cast an object to a type it isn't. The classic scenario is: you have an Object reference that's actually holding a String, and you try to cast it to an Integer — Java throws ClassCastException at runtime because the actual object is not an Integer. The safe pattern is to always check with instanceof before downcasting. Java 16 made this even cleaner with pattern matching: you write `if (obj instanceof String s)` and inside the if block, `s` is already cast for you. Upcasting — going from child to parent — is always safe and Java does it automatically.

questions.question: How do you convert a String to an int and an int to a String in Java?
questions.title: String to int and int to String Conversion in Java
questions.direct_answer: **String to int**: use `Integer.parseInt(str)` for a primitive int, or `Integer.valueOf(str)` for an Integer object. **Int to String**: use `String.valueOf(num)`, `Integer.toString(num)`, or concatenate with empty string `"" + num`. `parseInt` throws `NumberFormatException` if the string isn't a valid number.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java knowledge — type conversion is done in almost every real application
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Integer.parseInt on a non-numeric string without try-catch, or casting a String to int directly (which doesn't work)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish parseInt (returns primitive) vs valueOf (returns Integer object), and mention NumberFormatException handling

sections.title: String ↔ int Conversion
Key Points
sections.content:
- `Integer.parseInt(str)` → returns primitive `int`
- `Integer.valueOf(str)` → returns `Integer` object (uses Integer cache for small values)
- `String.valueOf(int)` → int to String, handles `null` gracefully
- `"" + number` works but creates an extra String object — less readable
- Always handle `NumberFormatException` when parsing user input
- Similarly: `Double.parseDouble()`, `Long.parseLong()`, `Boolean.parseBoolean()`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To convert a String to an int, you use `Integer.parseInt()` which gives you a primitive int, or `Integer.valueOf()` which gives you an Integer object. The important thing is to handle `NumberFormatException` — if someone passes in a string that isn't actually a number, it will throw. For the reverse — int to String — the cleanest way is `String.valueOf(number)` or `Integer.toString(number)`. You'll also see `"" + number` in code, which works but creates an extra object and isn't as readable. The same patterns apply for other numeric types: `Double.parseDouble()`, `Long.parseLong()`, and so on.

questions.question: What happens when you cast a double 9.99 to an int in Java — does it round or truncate?
questions.title: Truncation vs Rounding in Java double to int Cast
questions.direct_answer: Java **truncates** (not rounds) when casting a double to int. `(int) 9.99` gives `9`, and `(int) -3.7` gives `-3` (not -4). The fractional part is simply discarded. To round properly, use `Math.round()` first.

interviewer_intent.testing: A classic output prediction gotcha — truncation vs rounding is surprising to many freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting (int) 9.9 to give 10 — it gives 9; truncation always goes toward zero
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Math.round() for proper rounding, Math.ceil() and Math.floor() for ceiling/floor operations

sections.title: Truncation in Type Casting
Key Points
sections.content:
- `(int)` cast **truncates** toward zero — drops the fractional part
- `Math.round(d)` rounds to nearest integer (0.5 rounds up)
- `Math.ceil(d)` rounds up to the nearest integer
- `Math.floor(d)` rounds down to the nearest integer
- For negative numbers: `(int) -3.7 = -3` (toward zero, not -4)
- Truncation can cause bugs in calculations — always be explicit about whether you want truncation or rounding

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java truncates — it just chops off the decimal part. So `(int) 9.99` gives you 9, not 10. This is true regardless of how close to the next integer you are. For negative numbers, truncation goes toward zero — `(int) -3.7` gives -3, not -4. If you actually need to round, you use `Math.round()` which returns a long for double input. For ceiling — always round up — use `Math.ceil()`. For floor — always round down — use `Math.floor()`. The cast itself never rounds; it always just drops the fractional part.

questions.question: What is implicit type promotion in Java arithmetic expressions?
questions.title: Implicit Type Promotion in Java Arithmetic
questions.direct_answer: **Implicit type promotion** occurs when Java automatically converts smaller types to larger ones before arithmetic operations. `byte`, `short`, and `char` values are always promoted to `int` before any arithmetic. If either operand is `long`, `float`, or `double`, the other operand is promoted to match.

interviewer_intent.testing: A subtle but frequently tested Java behavior — byte + byte gives int, not byte
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming `byte b = 1 + 2;` works — it does only because 1+2 is a compile-time constant. `byte b = b1 + b2;` doesn't compile without a cast
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the byte + byte → int promotion rule and why you need an explicit cast to store back in a byte

sections.title: Type Promotion Rules
Key Points
sections.content:
- `byte`, `short`, `char` are **always promoted to int** before arithmetic
- Adding two bytes gives an int, not a byte
- If any operand is `long`, result is `long`; if `float`, result is `float`; if `double`, result is `double`
- Integer division always truncates: `7 / 2 = 3`
- To get floating-point division, cast one operand: `(double) 7 / 2 = 3.5`
- This is a frequent source of subtle bugs in calculation code

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java automatically promotes smaller types before doing arithmetic. The rule is: byte, short, and char are always promoted to int first, before any operation. So if you add two bytes, the result is actually an int, not a byte — and you'll get a compile error if you try to store it back in a byte without an explicit cast. For mixed-type arithmetic, the smaller type always gets promoted to the larger: int + long gives long, int + double gives double. The classic gotcha this causes is integer division: `7 / 2` gives `3`, not `3.5`. To get decimal division, at least one operand must be a floating-point type.

questions.question: What is the difference between Integer.parseInt() and (int) casting for String to int conversion?
questions.title: parseInt() vs Direct Cast for String to int in Java
questions.direct_answer: You **cannot** directly cast a String to an int with `(int)` — this causes a compile error because String and int are unrelated types. `Integer.parseInt()` is the correct method that parses the String's characters into a numeric value. These are fundamentally different operations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate truly understands type casting (related type hierarchy) vs parsing (converting string representation)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to do `int n = (int) "42"` — this is a compile error, not a runtime error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that casting works within type hierarchies (numeric types, or up/down an inheritance chain) while parsing is a text-to-number interpretation operation

sections.title: Casting vs Parsing
Key Points
sections.content:
- `(int) someString` is a **compile-time error** — String and int have no relationship
- **Casting** requires the types to be related (numeric types, or inheritance relationship)
- **Parsing** is text interpretation: `Integer.parseInt()`, `Double.parseDouble()`, etc.
- String → numeric conversion always requires a parsing method, never a direct cast
- char can be cast to int: `(int) 'A'` gives 65 (ASCII value) — this IS a valid cast

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: These are completely different operations. Casting means converting between compatible types — like casting a long to an int, or casting a parent reference to a child type. It only works when there's a type hierarchy relationship. String and int have no relationship, so you simply cannot cast between them — the compiler rejects it. Parsing is a different concept: `Integer.parseInt()` reads the text content of the string and converts its character sequence into an integer value. So for String to number, you always parse, never cast. One interesting edge case: you CAN cast a char to int because char is technically a numeric type — `(int) 'A'` gives you 65, the ASCII value.
